Two-part model for panel cost data

Source: R/twopart.R
twopart.Rd

Fits the two-part model of Duan et al. (1983), the standard model for health care expenditures with a mass of zeros: a binary model for P(y > 0) on all observations, and a model for E[y | y > 0] on the positive observations. The unconditional mean is E[y] = P(y > 0) * E[y | y > 0].

Usage

twopart(
  formula,
  data,
  index,
  binary_formula = NULL,
  model = c("pooling", "random"),
  link = c("probit", "logit"),
  positive = c("gamma", "lognormal"),
  retransform = c("smearing", "normal"),
  correlated = FALSE,
  cre = FALSE,
  weights = NULL,
  vcov = c("classical", "HC1", "cluster"),
  R = 21,
  maxit = 100,
  tol = 1e-10
)

Arguments

formula

model formula for the positive part, e.g. cost ~ age + treatment; also used for the binary part unless binary_formula is given

data

a data.frame

index

length-1 or length-2 character vector of panel index columns

binary_formula

optional right-hand-side formula for the binary part, e.g. ~ age + treatment + smoker

model

"pooling" or "random", used for both parts

link

link of the binary part, "probit" or "logit"

positive

"gamma" (gamma GLM, log link) or "lognormal" (linear model for log(y))

retransform

for positive = "lognormal": "smearing" or "normal"

correlated

logical; with model = "random" and positive = "lognormal", let the random intercepts of the two parts be correlated and fit them jointly

cre

logical; add individual means of the time-varying regressors to both parts

weights

optional observation weights (model = "pooling" only): the name of a column of data or a numeric vector with one value per row of data

vcov

covariance type passed to panglm() for both parts

R, maxit, tol

passed to panglm()

Value

an object of class "twopart" with components binary and positive (the two panglm() fits), retransformation (the factor phi, 1 for the gamma part) and the settings used. Methods: print, summary, coef, vcov, confint, predict, fitted, logLik, nobs, partialeffects(), tidy and glance.

Details

The positive part is either a gamma GLM with a log link (positive = "gamma", no retransformation needed) or a linear model for log(y) (positive = "lognormal"). For the log model, E[y | y > 0] = exp(x'beta) * phi needs a retransformation factor phi: Duan's smearing estimate, the (weighted) mean of the exponentiated log-scale residuals (retransform = "smearing"), or the normal-theory factor exp(sigma^2 / 2) (retransform = "normal"; with model = "random", sigma^2 is the sum of the individual and idiosyncratic variance components). Both assume homoskedastic log-scale errors.

With model = "random" each part has its own random intercept and the parts are estimated separately; the combined mean multiplies the two population-averaged means, which assumes the two random intercepts are independent. With correlated = TRUE (random effects, lognormal positive part) the two random intercepts are instead bivariate normal with correlation rho and both parts are estimated jointly by maximum likelihood (Van Ourti 2004): individuals with a high propensity to use care may also have high spending when they do. The positive-part random intercept is integrated out in closed form and the binary-part one by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Predictions then integrate over the joint distribution (normal-theory retransformation). A likelihood-ratio test of rho = 0 compares logLik() with the separate fit. cre = TRUE adds the individual means of the time-varying regressors (computed over all observations of the individual, including zeros) to both parts, the Mundlak correlated random effects device.

Validation

Both parts are panglm() fits and share its validation. The package tests also check that the pooled two-part prediction is the product of the two stats::glm() fits, the smearing retransformation of the lognormal part, and the correlated random-intercept likelihood against two-dimensional numerical integration.

References

Duan, N., Manning, W. G., Morris, C. N. and Newhouse, J. P. (1983). A comparison of alternative models for the demand for medical care. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 1, 115-126. doi:10.1080/07350015.1983.10509330

Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 78, 605-610. doi:10.1080/01621459.1983.10478017

Van Ourti, T. (2004). Measuring horizontal inequity in Belgian health care using a Gaussian random effects two part count data model. Health Economics, 13, 705-724. doi:10.1002/hec.869

See also

predict.twopart(), confint.twopart() and partialeffects() for the fitted model, tidy-methods for tidy() and glance().

Other panel models: panfmm(), panfmmselect(), panglm(), pangmm(), panhurdle(), paniv(), panqr(), panselect()

Examples

data(copd)
set.seed(1)
copd$cost <- ifelse(copd$exacerbations > 0,
                    exp(6 + 0.1 * copd$crp + rnorm(nrow(copd), 0, 0.5)), 0)
tp <- twopart(cost ~ treatment + age + crp, data = copd,
              index = c("id", "visit"), positive = "gamma")
summary(tp)
#>
